raw_response.country: Multiple countries referenced in overview (Netherlands, Uganda, Iran, Ghana, Zambia, and seven African countries; no primary study site)

criterion_notes.c1: The paper focuses thematically on the delivery of drinking water supply and sanitation services to the urban poor in slums and peri-urban areas.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper qualifies (plain=yes) because it discusses institutional, governance, and regulatory arrangements around utility performance benchmarking and multi-stakeholder pro-poor service delivery. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is not satisfied (narrow=no): the paper's core topic is organisational performance benchmarking as a monitoring and management tool rather than an empirical analysis of a rule-type mechanism directly governing household access, while references to legislation, regulators, utility mandates, tariffs, and subsidies appear only as unanalysed background or brief previews of other articles in the special issue. Regardless, under both readings the overall decision is exclude because Criterion 3 (empirical evidence) fails.
criterion_notes.c3: This article is an editorial introduction and high-level reflection for a journal special issue arising from the PROBE project. Sections 1-5 present conceptual discussion and general bullet-point lessons without primary data, sample description, or empirical methods (explicitly deferring framework and empirical details to subsequent articles in the issue), and Section 6 summarises the ten other papers in the special issue. It is neither an empirical study nor a systematic empirical synthesis (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: No empirical access, connection, continuity, or affordability outcomes are measured or reported by this introductory overview itself; outcomes are only mentioned in narrative previews of other papers in the special issue.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the paper is a non-empirical special-issue introduction and narrative reflection, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sample, operationalised exposure, or measured outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: The full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: A dedicated benchmarking system to assess the availability of water supply and sanitation services for the urban poor will be explained.

The pro-poor benchmarking (PROBE) project carried out by UNESCO-IHE with support of The Netherlands Ministry of Development Cooperation developed a supplementary benchmarking framework with five perspectives and thirteen indicators that incorporates the common approaches, systems and technologies for the provision of water and sanitation services to the poor. The details will be presented in the paper of Murungi and Blokland below.
Benchmarking in the water supply and sanitation sector is a tool for performance improvement and allows us to compare and enhance the performance of water utilities and the sector as a whole.

The research focused on defining and testing benchmarking systems that covers the array of measures that facilitate sustainable access to improved services for the poor. These measures may be of a legal, institutional, organisational, technical, or financial nature.
The first paper after this introduction by Nalwoga and van Dijk reviews existing organisational performance measurement models.

raw_response.rationale: Van Dijk and Blokland (2016) is an introductory overview and reflection piece for a special issue of the International Journal of Water on benchmarking pro-poor water and sanitation service delivery (the PROBE project). It contains no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology, and no systematic synthesis methods, instead offering conceptual reflections on utility benchmarking, high-level lessons learned, and narrative summaries of the ten other articles in the special issue. It is therefore excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence) under both the narrow 2026-10-13 reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
